A hypocrite is a person who says one thing but does another — specifically when it comes to beliefs, values, or moral standards.

More precisely: a hypocrite claims to hold certain values or standards, but their actual behavior directly contradicts those claims. There is a gap — often a wide, obvious one — between what they preach and what they practice.
A Simple, Clear Example

Imagine a man who tells everyone around him:

"Lying is wrong. Honesty is the most important value a person can have."

He says this often, loudly, and with great confidence. He even criticizes others for being dishonest.

But behind closed doors, this same man lies regularly — to his friends, his family, his boss — whenever it benefits him.

That man is a hypocrite.

He presents himself as a person who values honesty. But his actual behavior proves he does not truly live by that value. He wears a mask of virtue that his real actions tear off.
The Two Ingredients of a Hypocrite

Every hypocrite has two things working together:

  1. A claim — something they publicly say they believe in, stand for, or practice. This could be a moral value (honesty, kindness, fairness), a lifestyle choice, a religious belief, a political stance, or any standard of behavior.
  2. A contradiction — their actual behavior privately or quietly goes against that very claim.

Remove either one, and you don't have a hypocrite. A person who does bad things but never claimed to be good is not a hypocrite — they're just flawed. A hypocrite is specifically someone who sets up a standard for themselves (or others) and then secretly or openly breaks it.
A Crucial Nuance: Hypocrisy vs. Human Weakness

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand, and many people confuse it.

Consider someone who genuinely believes in healthy eating. They try their best, but one stressed night they eat junk food. They feel guilty. They didn't want to do it. They're trying again tomorrow.

That is NOT a hypocrite. That is a human being struggling.

A hypocrite is different. A hypocrite typically:

  • Has little or no intention of actually following the standard they preach, or
  • Applies the standard strictly to others while freely excusing themselves from it, or
  • Knowingly and repeatedly does the exact opposite of what they claim to believe, without guilt or private acknowledgment of the contradiction.

The key signal is deliberate inconsistency — knowingly living by a different rule than the one you publicly advertise.
The "Judge Others, Excuse Yourself" Pattern

One of the most common forms of hypocrisy involves double standards — judging other people harshly for the very thing you do yourself.

For example:

  • A politician who campaigns loudly against corruption, but secretly accepts bribes.
  • A person who lectures friends about the importance of being on time, but is always late themselves.
  • Someone who tells others not to gossip, and then gossips the moment those people leave the room.

In each case, the hypocrite holds others to a standard they refuse to hold themselves to. This double standard is the signature move of a hypocrite.
The Element of Performance

The word hypocrite carries a strong suggestion of performance — putting on a show for an audience.

A hypocrite is not just accidentally inconsistent. They are, in some meaningful sense, performing a version of themselves — a more virtuous, principled, or moral version — that doesn't match who they actually are. They want the reputation of being a good, principled person without actually doing the work of being one.

This is why hypocrisy feels like a form of deception. The hypocrite isn't just failing — they are actively presenting themselves as something they are not.
Degrees of Hypocrisy

Not all hypocrisy looks the same. It exists on a spectrum:

  • Mild hypocrisy: Someone who preaches work-life balance to their employees but constantly overworks themselves. The contradiction is real but may not involve serious moral harm.
  • Moderate hypocrisy: A person who publicly champions a charitable cause but donates nothing privately and is secretly indifferent to it.
  • Severe hypocrisy: A religious leader who preaches strict moral codes to their community while secretly committing serious moral violations. This kind involves a large, harmful gap between the public claim and private reality, often with real consequences for others.
Can a Hypocrite Know They're Being a Hypocrite?

Often, yes — and that's what makes it feel dishonest. Many hypocrites are fully aware of the gap between what they say and what they do; they simply choose to maintain the outward image anyway because it benefits them socially, professionally, or personally.

However, some hypocrites have a genuine blind spot — they apply critical thinking to others but not to themselves. They are so convinced of their own goodness that they don't notice, or refuse to notice, the contradiction. This kind of hypocrisy is less deliberately deceptive but no less real.
Related Word Forms (for completeness)

• Hypocrisy (noun) — the behavior or practice itself. "His hypocrisy was on full display."
  • Hypocritical (adjective) — used to describe a person, action, or statement that is characteristic of a hypocrite. "It was hypocritical of her to criticize laziness while never doing any work herself."
  • Hypocritically (adverb) — in a hypocritical manner. "He hypocritically condemned the very behavior he engaged in."
In One Sentence

If you ever need to recall this word quickly:

A hypocrite is someone who demands a standard of others — or presents one about themselves — that they do not actually follow in their own life.

That gap between the mask they wear and the reality underneath is what the word is entirely about.
